fixes.explanation: I see why you'd lean that way, friend. You'd think that many signs would settle it. But the Gospel of John says, “Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him.” (John 12:37) So the answer is False, and that's what makes the verse so striking.

That's it, friend. The writer says, “Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him.” (John 12:37) Signs piled up and the belief just wasn't there. So the answer is False.

Yes, friend. The writer says, “Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.” (John 12:41) Isaiah the prophet was talking about Jesus. That's a whole lot of looking ahead packed into one verse.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, so I get the pull. But the writer doesn't mention him here at all. The verse says Isaiah spoke because “…he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.” (John 12:41) The glory belongs to Jesus.

Elijah, a prophet of Israel, is a famous name, so I see how he slipped in there. But he isn't in this passage. The writer says Isaiah “…saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.” (John 12:41) So the blank is Jesus.

I wanted that to be true too, friend. But the writer says that because of the Pharisees, a strict Jewish religious group, “…they did not confess Him…” (John 12:42) They believed, but they kept it quiet. So the answer is False.

That's right. The Gospel of John tells us many of the leaders believed in Him, “But because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him…” (John 12:42) The belief was real, but the confessing out loud didn't happen. I think that's a heavy spot to be in.

Yes, friend. The writer says they stayed quiet “…for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue.” (John 12:42) That's the fear the text names. It's a quiet kind of pressure, and I think plenty of people feel something like it.

That's a scary thought, but the writer doesn't say it here. The text says they feared “…that they would be put out of the synagogue.” (John 12:42) Prison never comes up. So the fear was being put out.

Nice try, friend, but a feast seat isn't in this verse. The text says the leaders did not confess Him “…for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue.” (John 12:42) That's the fear in this passage. Keep your eyes on that verse.

That's it. The writer says, “For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.” (John 12:43) It's a plain sentence, and it's easy to see ourselves in it. I know I like a compliment on a good batch.

Families matter a lot, but the writer doesn't say that here. The text says, “For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.” (John 12:43) The text points to praise. So the answer is praise from people.

Money and land are a fair guess, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The writer says, “For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.” (John 12:43) The thing they loved more was praise. That one's the answer.
Yes, friend. Jesus cries out, “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me.” (John 12:44) Believing in Jesus reaches the One who sent Him too.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me.” (John 12:45) Just before this, He said that believing in Him means believing in the One who sent Him (John 12:44). So when someone looks at Jesus, they are seeing the One who sent Him.

I get why you'd say that, friend. But Jesus says, “As for anyone who hears My words and does not keep them, I do not judge him.” (John 12:47) So Jesus says the opposite: He does not judge that person. The answer is False.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world.” (John 12:47) He has just said He doesn't judge the one who hears His words and doesn't keep them. Judging isn't why He came. He came to save.

That's a fair guess, but it's not the word Jesus uses. He says, “For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world.” (John 12:47) He doesn't say He came to test the world. He sets judging against saving, and the blank is save.

Rule makes sense as a guess, but Jesus doesn't use it. He says, “For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world.” (John 12:47) He doesn't say He came to rule the world. He puts judging next to saving, and saving is the word He picks.

That's a fair guess, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “So I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say.” (John 12:50) Partly would mean some of His words came from somewhere else. Exactly means all of them come from the Father, who commanded Him what to say and how to say it (John 12:49).
